items.title: Kernel inclusion implies weak containment
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group and let $\pi,\rho$ be unitary representations with $C^*\ker\rho\subseteq C^*\ker\pi$. Then $\pi\prec\rho$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** AC, an LCH group $G$, unitary representations $\pi,\rho$ with $\ker\rho\subseteq\ker\pi$, a unit vector $\xi\in H_\pi$, a compact set $Q\subseteq G$ and $\epsilon>0$.

1.1 Let $k(g):=\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle$ and, for a convex combination $\theta=\sum_j\lambda_j\omega_{\eta_j}$ of normalized vector states of $B$ with associated coefficient $k_\theta(g):=\sum_j\lambda_j\langle\rho(g)\eta_j,\eta_j\rangle$, and for $f\in C_c(G)$ with $\int_Gf=1$ and $f\ge0$, one has $|k(g)-\langle\pi(f)\xi,\xi\rangle_g|\le(2(1-\operatorname{Re}\varphi(f)))^{1/2}$ and $|k_\theta(g)-\theta(L_gf)|\le(2(1-\operatorname{Re}\theta(f)))^{1/2}$ for every $g$, where $\langle\pi(f)\xi,\xi\rangle_g:=\int_Gf(h)k(gh)\,dh$ and $\theta(L_gf)=\int_Gf(h)k_\theta(gh)\,dh$ by [F4]. Indeed, $|k(g)-k(gh)|\le(2(1-\operatorname{Re}k(h)))^{1/2}$ by [F3], and Cauchy–Schwarz for the probability measure $f\,dh$ gives $\int_Gf(h)(2(1-\operatorname{Re}k(h)))^{1/2}dh\le(2(1-\int_Gf(h)\operatorname{Re}k(h)\,dh))^{1/2}=(2(1-\operatorname{Re}\varphi(f)))^{1/2}$; the same computation applies to $k_\theta$, whose summands satisfy the same estimate by [F3] and Cauchy–Schwarz for the weights $\lambda_j$. [F3, F4]

1.2 Fix $f\in C_c(G)$. The set $\{L_gf:g\in Q\}$ is compact in $L^1(G)$ by [F4], hence its image under the continuous map into $C^*(G)$ is compact; since $\theta_i(\rho(b))\to\widetilde\varphi(\rho(b))$ for every $b\in C^*(G)$ by [F1] and [F2], a finite $\delta$-net argument gives $\sup_{g\in Q}|\theta_i(L_gf)-\varphi(L_gf)|\to0$, where $\varphi(L_gf)=\widetilde\varphi(\rho(L_gf))$. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Consequently $k$ is a compact-uniform limit of the coefficients $k_\theta$: enlarging the given compact set $Q$ to $Q\cup\{e\}$ if necessary, and given $\epsilon>0$, choose $f\in C_c(G)$ with $f\ge0$, $\int f=1$ and support so small that $1-\operatorname{Re}k(h)<\epsilon$ on it, so that $1-\operatorname{Re}\varphi(f)<\epsilon$; eventually $1-\operatorname{Re}\theta_i(f)<2\epsilon$ by step 1.2 applied at $e$, and then $\sup_Q|k-k_{\theta_i}|\le(2\epsilon)^{1/2}+\sup_Q|\theta_i(L_gf)-\varphi(L_gf)|+(4\epsilon)^{1/2}$, which is $<4\sqrt\epsilon$ once $i$ is large: the first and third terms sum to $(\sqrt2+2)\sqrt\epsilon<4\sqrt\epsilon$, and the middle term tends to zero, by steps 1.1 and 1.2. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Therefore every normalized diagonal coefficient of $\pi$ is a compact-uniform limit of finite sums of diagonal coefficients of $\rho$; for an arbitrary vector $\xi\ne0$ the coefficient $c_{\xi,\xi}=\|\xi\|^2c_{\xi/\|\xi\|,\xi/\|\xi\|}$ is a nonnegative multiple of a normalized one and the approximating sums scale by the same factor, so by [F1]–[F2] and the definition of weak containment $\pi\prec\rho$. [step 2.1]

4.1 The Axiom of Choice is used for the geometric separation behind the vector-state approximation of step 2.1 and is inherited from the whole chain ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). [given, F2] ∎

items.title: Weak containment implies kernel inclusion
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group and let $\pi\prec\rho$ (weak containment). Then $C^*\ker\rho\subseteq C^*\ker\pi$; more precisely $\|\pi(a)\|\le\|\rho(a)\|$ for every $a\in C^*(G)$.
items.strategy: It suffices to prove the norm inequality on the dense $*$-subalgebra $L^1(G)$ and extend by density. Fix a unit vector $\xi\in H_\pi$ and a compactly supported continuous $f$ with support in a compact $Q$. Given $\epsilon>0$, weak containment supplies $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_n$ with $\sup_{g\in Q}|\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle-\sum_j\langle\rho(g)\eta_j,\eta_j\rangle|<\epsilon$; integrating against $f$ gives $|\langle\pi(f)\xi,\xi\rangle-\sum_j\langle\rho(f)\eta_j,\eta_j\rangle|\le\epsilon\|f\|_1$. Since $e\in Q$ (enlarge $Q$), the total mass satisfies $\sum_j\|\eta_j\|^2\le1+\epsilon$, whence $|\langle\pi(f)\xi,\xi\rangle|\le(1+\epsilon)\|\rho(f)\|+\epsilon\|f\|_1$; letting $\epsilon\to0$ and taking the supremum over unit $\xi$ on the self-adjoint element $f^*f$ ([[lem-quadratic-form-of-a-self-adjoint-operator-attains-the-norm]]) gives $\|\pi(f)\|^2=\|\pi(f^*f)\|\le\|\rho(f^*f)\|=\|\rho(f)\|^2$. Density of $C_c(G)$ in $L^1(G)$ and of $L^1(G)$ in $C^*(G)$ finishes. AC is declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; it enters through the quadratic-form norm attainment and the dominated-operator comparison used in the net argument.

items.title: The canonical map from the full to the reduced group C star algebra
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group. The integrated form of the left regular representation extends to a surjective $*$-homomorphism $$\lambda_G:C^*(G)\twoheadrightarrow C^*_r(G),$$ the identity on $L^1(G)$; conversely $\lambda_G(f)\mapsto\pi(f)$ defines a $*$-homomorphism $C^*_r(G)\to C^*_\pi(G)$ for every unitary representation $\pi$ whose kernel contains $C^*\ker\lambda_G$. In particular $C^*_r(G)$ is a quotient of $C^*(G)$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** AC, an LCH group $G$, the integrated forms $\lambda_G(f)$ and $\pi(f)$, and the C\*-algebras $C^*(G)$, $C^*_r(G)$, $C^*_\pi(G)$.

1.1 The integrated form of the regular representation extends to a star-homomorphism $\Lambda:C^*(G)\to\mathcal B(L^2(G))$ with $\Lambda(f)=\lambda_G(f)$ on $L^1(G)$, and $\Lambda$ is surjective onto $C^*_r(G)$: the extension exists by the universal property [F2] applied to the unitary representation $\lambda_G$, its image contains $\lambda_G(L^1(G))$ and is closed by [F3], hence contains the norm closure $C^*_r(G)$ by [F4], while by construction the image is contained in $C^*_r(G)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

1.2 Let $\pi$ be a unitary representation of $G$ with $\ker\lambda_G\subseteq\ker\pi$ (kernels of the extended representations on $C^*(G)$). The assignment $\lambda_G(f)\mapsto\pi(f)$ for $f\in L^1(G)$ is well defined and linear, multiplicative and star-preserving where defined, because $\lambda_G(f)=\lambda_G(h)$ means $f-h\in\ker\lambda_G\subseteq\ker\pi$; To justify its relative norm bound, factor the bounded extension $\pi$ through $Q=C^*(G)/\ker\lambda_G$. The induced map $\dot\pi$ is bounded because $\|\dot\pi(a+\ker\lambda_G)\|\le\|\pi\|\inf_{k\in\ker\lambda_G}\|a+k\|$. The map $\dot\Lambda:Q\to C^*_r(G)$ induced by step 1.1 is injective, surjective and isometric by [F3]. Hence $T=\dot\pi\circ\dot\Lambda^{-1}$ is a bounded star-homomorphism, and is contractive by the C*-quotient supplier [F3]. Its image lies in $C^*_\pi(G)$ by density of the integrated forms. Its restriction is exactly $\lambda_G(f)\mapsto\pi(f)$, proving the assertion without inferring relative boundedness from two separate $L^1$ bounds. [F2, F3, F4]

2.1 In particular $C^*_r(G)$ is a quotient of $C^*(G)$, namely the quotient by the closed two-sided ideal $\ker\lambda_G$, and the second assertion of the statement is the factorization of any representation whose kernel contains that ideal through this quotient. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the full-norm completion and the representation correspondence; the quotient and density arguments use no further choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

items.title: Irreducible weak containment in a family selects one coefficient
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group, $(\rho_s)_{s\in S}$ a set-indexed family of nonzero unitary representations and $\pi$ an irreducible unitary representation. If $\pi\prec\bigoplus_{s\in S}\rho_s$, then for every unit $\xi\in H_\pi$, every compact $Q\subseteq G$ and every $\epsilon>0$, there are $s\in S$ and a unit $\eta\in H_{\rho_s}$ with $\sup_{g\in Q}|\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle-\langle\rho_s(g)\eta,\eta\rangle|<\epsilon$. For any finite family of coefficients of $\pi$, a single $s$ can be chosen to approximate all of them on $Q$ by coefficients of $\rho_s$ (with separately chosen vectors, without a normalization requirement). In particular, if every $\rho_s$ is irreducible, then $\pi$ lies in the Fell closure of $\{[\rho_s]:s\in S\}$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** AC, an LCH group $G$ with left Haar measure, a family $(\rho_s)_{s\in S}$ of nonzero unitary representations, an irreducible unitary representation $\pi$ with $\pi\prec\widehat\bigoplus_s\rho_s$, and $A=C^*(G)$.

1.1 If $S=\varnothing$ the direct sum is the zero representation and $\pi\prec0$ is impossible, because the unit coefficient $\langle\pi(\cdot)\xi,\xi\rangle$ takes the value $1$ at $e$ and cannot be approximated by $0$ on the compact set $\{e\}$; hence $S\ne\varnothing$ and $F:=\{\omega_{\rho_s,\eta}:s\in S,\ \eta\in H_{\rho_s},\ \|\eta\|=1\}$ is a nonempty subset of $K$ by [F3]. The functional $\omega:=\omega_{\pi,\xi}$ lies in $K$, has norm $1$ and is extreme in $K$ by [F4]. [F2, F3, F4]

2.1 For every compact $Q\subseteq G$ and $\epsilon>0$, a convex combination of $F$ approximates $\omega$ within $\epsilon$ on $Q$. Fix $0<\delta<1/4$ so that $4\delta/(1-2\delta)<\epsilon$, and apply [F1] on $Q\cup\{e\}$ with error $\delta$. This gives finitely many vectors $\eta_l$ in the Hilbert direct sum. Truncate each $\eta_l$ to finitely many summands so that the sum of the uniform coefficient errors is $<\delta$: this is possible by norm density of finitely supported vectors and the estimate $|c_{\eta_l,\eta_l}-c_{v_l,v_l}|\le(\|\eta_l\|+\|v_l\|)\|\eta_l-v_l\|$. Write the resulting finite coefficient sum as $\psi(g)=\sum_{l,s}\langle\rho_s(g)v_l^{(s)},v_l^{(s)}\rangle$, retaining each pair $(l,s)$ separately. Then $\sup_{Q\cup\{e\}}|\psi-\omega|<2\delta$. Put $t=\sum_{l,s}\|v_l^{(s)}\|^2=\psi(e)$, so $|t-1|<2\delta$ and $t>0$. Dividing each nonzero vector by its norm shows that $\phi:=\psi/t$ is the convex combination of normalized vector states with weights $\|v_l^{(s)}\|^2/t$. Finally $|\phi-\omega|\le(|\psi-\omega|+|1-t||\omega|)/t<4\delta/(1-2\delta)<\epsilon$ on $Q$. [F1, F2, F10, step 1.1]

3.1 The functional $\omega$ lies in the weak-\* closure $C$ of $\operatorname{co}(F)$ in $A^*$. Let $f_1,\dots,f_N\in L^1(G)$ and $\eta>0$. By [F8] choose compactly supported continuous $g_i$ with $\|f_i-g_i\|_1<\eta/12$, and put $Q:=\bigcup_i\operatorname{supp}g_i$, a compact set with $2\int_{G\setminus Q}|f_i|<\eta/3$ for every $i$. By step 2.1 choose $\phi\in\operatorname{co}(F)$ with $\sup_Q|\phi-\omega|<\eta/(3+3\sum_i\|f_i\|_1)$; then, since $|\phi-\omega|\le2$ on $G$ and each $\phi\in\operatorname{co}(F)$ lies in $K$ by convexity [F4], $\bigl|\int_Gf_i(\phi-\omega)\bigr|\le\|f_i\|_1\sup_Q|\phi-\omega|+2\int_{G\setminus Q}|f_i|<\eta$ for every $i$. The image of $L^1(G)$ is dense in $A$ and $\|\phi\|,\|\omega\|\le1$, so the same conclusion holds with $f_i$ replaced by arbitrary $a_i\in A$: every weak-\* neighbourhood of $\omega$ meets $\operatorname{co}(F)$, that is, $\omega\in C$. [F4, F8, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $C=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(F)\subseteq K$ is weak-\* closed and convex and $K$ is compact by [F4], $C$ is compact. By step 1.1 the functional $\omega$ is extreme in $K$ and $\omega\in C$ by step 3.1, so $\omega$ is extreme in $C$; Milman's converse [F5] applied to the compact convex set $C=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(F)$ gives $\omega\in\overline F$. Hence there is a net $(\phi_\alpha)\subseteq F$ converging to $\omega$ in the weak-\* topology of $A^*$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Part 1 of the statement holds. Each $\phi_\alpha$ is $\omega_{\rho_{s(\alpha)},\eta(\alpha)}$ for some $s(\alpha)\in S$ and unit vector $\eta(\alpha)\in H_{\rho_{s(\alpha)}}$; its restriction to $L^1(G)$ is integration against the normalized coefficient $\psi_\alpha(g)=\langle\rho_{s(\alpha)}(g)\eta(\alpha),\eta(\alpha)\rangle\in P_1(G)$, and $\int_Gf\psi_\alpha\to\int_Gf\,\omega_{\pi,\xi}(g)\,dg$ for every $f\in L^1(G)$ because $\phi_\alpha\to\omega$ weak-\* on $A$. By Raikov's theorem [F6] the net $(\psi_\alpha)$ converges to the coefficient $\langle\pi(\cdot)\xi,\xi\rangle$ uniformly on compact subsets, so for the prescribed compact $Q$ and $\epsilon$ some $\alpha$ has $\sup_Q|\psi_\alpha(g)-\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle|<\epsilon$; with $s=s(\alpha)$ and $\eta=\eta(\alpha)$ this is the first assertion. [F6, step 4.1]

6.1 Part 2 of the statement holds. Fix a unit vector $\xi\in H_\pi$, which exists since $\pi$ is irreducible and hence acts on a nonzero space. For each $i$ with $\xi_i\ne0$, cyclicity [F9] (applied to the nonzero vector $\xi$) gives $c_{ij}\in\mathbb C$ and $x_{ij}\in G$ with $v_i:=\sum_jc_{ij}\pi(x_{ij})\xi$ satisfying $\|\xi_i-v_i\|<\epsilon/(2(1+\|\xi_i\|+\|v_i\|))$, so that $(\|\xi_i\|+\|v_i\|)\|\xi_i-v_i\|<\epsilon/2$ by [F10]; for $\xi_i=0$ take $v_i=0$. Put $M_i=(\sum_j|c_{ij}|)^2$ and $M=1+\max_iM_i$, and apply part 1 to the compact set $\bigcup_{i,j,k}x_{ik}^{-1}Qx_{ij}$ with radius $\delta=\epsilon/(2M)$: this gives $s\in S$ and a unit vector $\eta\in H_{\rho_s}$ with $\sup|\langle\pi(h)\xi,\xi\rangle-\langle\rho_s(h)\eta,\eta\rangle|<\delta$ over that union. Set $w_i:=\sum_jc_{ij}\rho_s(x_{ij})\eta$. Expanding, $\langle\pi(g)v_i,v_i\rangle=\sum_{j,k}c_{ij}\bar c_{ik}\langle\pi(x_{ik}^{-1}gx_{ij})\xi,\xi\rangle$ and $\langle\rho_s(g)w_i,w_i\rangle=\sum_{j,k}c_{ij}\bar c_{ik}\langle\rho_s(x_{ik}^{-1}gx_{ij})\eta,\eta\rangle$, so on $Q$ the two coefficients differ by at most $\delta M_i<\epsilon/2$ by [F2] and [F10]; combined with the perturbation bound $|\langle\pi(g)\xi_i,\xi_i\rangle-\langle\pi(g)v_i,v_i\rangle|\le(\|\xi_i\|+\|v_i\|)\|\xi_i-v_i\|<\epsilon/2$ of [F10] this yields $\sup_Q|\langle\pi(g)\xi_i,\xi_i\rangle-\langle\rho_s(g)w_i,w_i\rangle|<\epsilon$ for every $i$. [F2, F9, F10, step 5.1]

7.1 Part 3 of the statement holds. Let $W(\pi;\phi_1,\dots,\phi_N,Q,\epsilon)$ be a basic Fell neighbourhood of $[\pi]$ [F7]; each $\phi_i$ is a finite sum $\sum_{l=1}^{n_i}\langle\pi(\cdot)\xi_{i,l},\xi_{i,l}\rangle$ of diagonal coefficients. Applying step 6.1 to the finite list of all vectors $\xi_{i,l}$ with precision $\epsilon/(1+\max_in_i)$ produces a single $s\in S$ and vectors $\eta_{i,l}\in H_{\rho_s}$ with $\sup_Q|\langle\pi(g)\xi_{i,l},\xi_{i,l}\rangle-\langle\rho_s(g)\eta_{i,l},\eta_{i,l}\rangle|<\epsilon/n_i$ for all $i,l$; summing over $l$ shows that each $\phi_i$ is within $\epsilon$ on $Q$ of the finite sum $\sum_l\langle\rho_s(\cdot)\eta_{i,l},\eta_{i,l}\rangle$ of functions of positive type associated to $\rho_s$. Hence $[\rho_s]\in W$; since every basic neighbourhood of $[\pi]$ is met by $\{[\rho_s]:s\in S\}$, the class $[\pi]$ lies in the closure of that set when all $\rho_s$ are irreducible (so that their classes lie in the dual). [F7, step 6.1]

8.1 The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the extreme-point supplier, the Hilbert direct sum, Raikov's theorem and the finitely many group elements selected in the cyclicity argument; the coefficient and convexity computations are choice-free ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). [given] ∎

items.title: Weak containment is equivalent to kernel inclusion
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group and let $\pi,\rho$ be unitary representations of $G$. Then $\pi\prec\rho$ if and only if $C^*\ker\rho\subseteq C^*\ker\pi$, where the kernels are taken in $C^*(G)$; equivalently $\pi\prec\rho$ iff $\|\pi(a)\|\le\|\rho(a)\|$ for every $a\in C^*(G)$. In particular weak equivalence of irreducibles is exactly equality of $C^*$-kernels, so the map $\kappa$ of [[def-primitive-ideal-space-of-a-group-c-star-algebra]] is well defined and its fibres are the weak equivalence classes.
items.strategy: The two implications are [[lem-weak-containment-implies-kernel-inclusion]] and [[lem-kernel-inclusion-implies-weak-containment]]. The norm-inequality form is the content of the first of them, and it is an immediate restatement in the presence of the correspondence [[thm-nondegenerate-representations-of-c-star-g-are-unitary-representations-of-g]]. This is Proposition 8.B.4 of [BeH–19] and Theorem F.4.4 of [BeHV–08]. AC is declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and is carried from the two implications proved above.

items.title: Normalized coefficient approximation for irreducible weak containment
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group, $\pi$ an irreducible unitary representation and $\rho$ a unitary representation with $\pi\prec\rho$. Then every normalized function of positive type $\phi$ associated to $\pi$ can be approximated, uniformly on compact subsets of $G$, by normalized functions of positive type associated to $\rho$ (a single one for each approximation step, not only by finite sums).
items.strategy: The hypothesis forces $\rho$ to be nonzero, since its zero coefficients cannot approximate a normalized coefficient at the identity. Apply [[lem-irreducible-weak-containment-in-a-family-selects-one-coefficient]] to the singleton family $S=\{s\}$ with $\rho_s=\rho$. Its proof places the irreducible vector functional in the weak-* compact positive contractive $C^*(G)$-functional ball, proves its extremality by a dominated-functional/Schur argument, applies Milman's converse to the union of individual vector functionals, and uses Raikov to obtain normalized coefficient approximation on compact subsets. This supplies explicitly the compactness and extremality steps in [BeHV–08, Proposition F.1.4], rather than assuming an unproved weak-* compactness theorem for $P_{\le1}(G)$. AC is inherited from that helper and declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

items.title: The kernel map is a homeomorphism onto the primitive ideal space
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group and let $\kappa:\widehat G\to\operatorname{Prim}(C^*(G))$, $[\pi]\mapsto C^*\ker\pi$. Then $\kappa$ is continuous and surjective, its fibres are exactly the weak-equivalence classes of irreducible representations ([[thm-weak-containment-is-equivalent-to-kernel-inclusion]]), and the induced bijection $\widehat G/\sim\,\to\operatorname{Prim}(C^*(G))$ is a homeomorphism when the quotient carries the quotient Fell topology ([[def-fell-topology-on-the-unitary-dual]], [[lem-fell-neighbourhoods-of-an-irreducible-representation-are-saturated-under-weak-equivalence]]) and $\operatorname{Prim}(C^*(G))$ carries the Jacobson topology ([[def-primitive-ideal-space-of-a-group-c-star-algebra]]).
items.strategy:
First prove the closure identity without appealing to this theorem. For $S\subseteq\widehat G$, if $\pi\in\overline S$, every finite-coefficient Fell neighbourhood meets $S$; its approximating sums are coefficients of representations in $S$, hence of $\bigoplus_S\sigma$. Thus $\pi\prec\bigoplus_S\sigma$. Conversely, that weak containment puts $\pi$ in $\overline S$ by the family-selection and simultaneous-coefficient argument of [[lem-irreducible-weak-containment-in-a-family-selects-one-coefficient]]. By [[thm-weak-containment-is-equivalent-to-kernel-inclusion]], these two directions give $\overline S=\{\pi:\kappa(\pi)\supseteq\bigcap_{\sigma\in S}\kappa(\sigma)\}=\kappa^{-1}(\overline{\kappa(S)}^{\rm Jac})$, using the Jacobson closure formula in [[def-primitive-ideal-space-of-a-group-c-star-algebra]]. For $S=\varnothing$ the intersection is $C^*(G)$ and the displayed set is empty since irreducible representations are nonzero and nondegenerate.

The representation correspondence [[thm-nondegenerate-representations-of-c-star-g-are-unitary-representations-of-g]] preserves irreducibility, so the definition of primitive ideal gives surjectivity of $\kappa$. Equal kernels are equivalent to mutual weak containment, so its fibres are exactly the stated classes. If $D$ is Jacobson closed, apply the closure identity to $S=\kappa^{-1}(D)$; surjectivity gives $\overline S=\kappa^{-1}(\overline D)=S$, proving continuity. Conversely, if $S$ is Fell closed, the identity says $S=\kappa^{-1}(\overline{\kappa(S)})$, so surjectivity gives $\kappa(S)=\overline{\kappa(S)}$; thus $\kappa$ is a closed surjection. Let $q:\widehat G\to\widehat G/\sim$ be the quotient. The induced bijection $\bar\kappa$ is continuous because $\kappa=\bar\kappa\circ q$ is continuous and $q$ has the quotient topology. If $E$ is closed in the quotient, $q^{-1}(E)$ is Fell closed, so $\bar\kappa(E)=\kappa(q^{-1}(E))$ is Jacobson closed. Hence the continuous bijection is closed and its inverse is continuous. This proves the full commissioned homeomorphism, including the formerly imported lifting half, from the two local helpers and the exact listed suppliers. Fell 1962 and [BeH–19, Propositions 8.B.3–8.B.4] are historical/source statements, not proof dependencies; Fell 1960 remains unread and is not consumed. AC is explicitly declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and inherited from the representation, weak-containment and family-selection suppliers.

items.title: Fell closure is characterized by weak containment
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group, $S\subseteq\widehat G$ and $\pi\in\widehat G$. Then $\pi$ lies in the Fell closure of $S$ if and only if $\pi\prec\bigoplus_{\sigma\in S}\sigma$. Equivalently, the Fell closure of $S$ is the set of all $\pi\in\widehat G$ whose $C^*$-kernel contains $\bigcap_{\sigma\in S}C^*\ker\sigma$.
items.strategy: The proof of [[thm-the-kernel-map-is-a-homeomorphism-onto-the-primitive-ideal-space]] establishes the identity $\overline S=\kappa^{-1}(\overline{\kappa(S)}^{\rm Jac})$ for arbitrary $S\subseteq\widehat G$, including the empty set. Import that proved identity. The Jacobson closure formula from [[def-primitive-ideal-space-of-a-group-c-star-algebra]] makes it $\overline S=\{\pi:C^*\ker\pi\supseteq\bigcap_{\sigma\in S}C^*\ker\sigma\}$. The direct sum acts componentwise, so $C^*\ker(\bigoplus_S\sigma)=\bigcap_{\sigma\in S}C^*\ker\sigma$, and [[thm-weak-containment-is-equivalent-to-kernel-inclusion]] gives the claimed weak-containment equivalence. The supplier proves the closure identity first by family selection and only then the homeomorphism, so this use is acyclic and does not infer closure lifting from a quotient homeomorphism alone. AC is inherited from that supplier and explicitly declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

items.title: Fell neighbourhoods of an irreducible representation are saturated under weak equivalence
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group and $\pi\in\widehat G$. In the Fell topology on $\widehat G$ there is a basis of neighbourhoods of $\pi$ consisting of the sets $\widetilde W(\pi;\phi_1,\dots,\phi_n,Q,\epsilon)$ of all $\rho\in\widehat G$ such that each $\phi_i$ is within $\epsilon$ on $Q$ of a single function of positive type associated to $\rho$. Consequently every Fell-open subset of $\widehat G$ is invariant under weak equivalence: if $\pi\in U$ and $\rho\sim\pi$ then $\rho\in U$.
items.strategy: A single-coefficient set $\widetilde W$ is contained in its finite-sum counterpart $W$. To prove it is a neighbourhood of the irreducible centre $\pi$, suppose otherwise. Every standard Fell neighbourhood of $\pi$ would meet the set $T=\widehat G\setminus\widetilde W$. Its coefficient approximations imply $\pi\prec\bigoplus_{\sigma\in T}\sigma$. By the simultaneous-coefficient conclusion of [[lem-irreducible-weak-containment-in-a-family-selects-one-coefficient]], one member of $T$ meets all the single-coefficient tests defining $\widetilde W$, a contradiction. Therefore $\widetilde W$ contains a standard Fell neighbourhood, and these sets form a neighbourhood basis. This argument supplies the precise finite-neighbourhood consequence of [BeHV–08, Proposition F.2.4]; it does not apply a global weak-containment lemma to a single finite test. For saturation, if $\rho\sim\pi$ and a Fell-open set contains $\pi$, choose a standard neighbourhood of $\pi$ inside it. The definition of $\pi\prec\rho$ puts $\rho$ in every such neighbourhood. The reverse containment of open-set memberships follows from $\rho\prec\pi$. Thus every open set is saturated. AC is inherited from the family helper and declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

items.title: Weak containment of the trivial representation and almost invariant vectors
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group and $(\pi,H)$ a unitary representation. Then $1_G\prec\pi$ if and only if for every compact $Q\subseteq G$ and every $\epsilon>0$ there is a unit vector $\xi\in H$ with $\sup_{g\in Q}\|\pi(g)\xi-\xi\|<\epsilon$. This is the statement that $\pi$ almost has invariant vectors.
items.strategy: For a unit vector $\xi$ and $g\in G$ one has $\|\pi(g)\xi-\xi\|^2=2(1-\operatorname{Re}\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle)$ and, by Cauchy–Schwarz applied to $1-\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle=\langle\xi-\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle$, $$|1-\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle|\le\|\pi(g)\xi-\xi\|=\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{Re}\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle)}$$ (the extract of [BeHV–08, Corollary F.1.5] prints the second inequality without the square and square root; the displayed form is the one used there). Hence uniform closeness of the coefficient $\langle\pi(\cdot)\xi,\xi\rangle$ to $1$ on $Q$ and the existence of an almost invariant unit vector are equivalent. Since $1_G$ is irreducible, [[lem-normalized-coefficient-approximation-for-irreducible-weak-containment]] reduces the definition of $1_G\prec\pi$ to approximation of its single normalized coefficient $1$ by normalized coefficients of $\pi$. This is [BeHV–08, Corollary F.1.5]. AC is declared and inherited from [[lem-normalized-coefficient-approximation-for-irreducible-weak-containment]], which assumes it; the dependency is declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

items.title: The unitary dual to primitive ideal map is continuous and surjective
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be an LCH group and let $\kappa:\widehat G\to\operatorname{Prim}(C^*(G))$, $\kappa([\pi])=C^*\ker\pi$. Then $\kappa$ is continuous for the Fell topology on $\widehat G$ and the Jacobson topology on $\operatorname{Prim}(C^*(G))$, and it is surjective. The induced map on weak equivalence classes is a homeomorphism onto $\operatorname{Prim}(C^*(G))$.
items.strategy: All assertions are the conclusions of [[thm-the-kernel-map-is-a-homeomorphism-onto-the-primitive-ideal-space]], whose local proof establishes the Fell/Jacobson closure identity by selection of a coefficient from one individual member of a family, then proves that $\kappa$ is a continuous closed surjection and that the induced bijection on weak-equivalence classes has continuous inverse. Thus the commissioned homeomorphism is supplied in full. AC is inherited from that theorem and explicitly declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

items.title: The unitary dual need not be Hausdorff
items.statement: Assume AC. There is a second-countable locally compact group whose unitary dual, with the Fell topology, is not Hausdorff. Explicitly, let $G=\mathbb R_{>0}\ltimes\mathbb R$ be the affine group of the line, with $(a,b)(a',b')=(aa',b+ab')$ and the topology of $\mathbb R_{>0}\times\mathbb R$, and let $\pi$ be the representation on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ given by $(\pi(a,b)\eta)(u)=e^{ibe^u}\eta(u+\log a)$. Then: (1) $\pi$ is a strongly continuous irreducible unitary representation and $\pi\not\simeq1_G$ (it is infinite dimensional); (2) every unitary character $\chi_t(a,b)=a^{it}$ ($t\in\mathbb R$) lies in the Fell closure of the singleton $\{\pi\}$, so in particular the trivial character $1_G=\chi_0$ does; (3) hence the singleton $\{\pi\}$ is not closed and $\widehat G$ is not a Hausdorff space. This is a direct local example of non-Hausdorff Fell topology; no classification of the whole unitary dual or claim about type I is required.
items.strategy:
The multiplication law and product topology make $G$ a second-countable LCH group. The operator formula is unitary by translation invariance of Lebesgue measure and the modulus-one multiplier. Direct composition gives $e^{ibe^u}e^{ib'e^{u+\log a}}=e^{i(b+ab')e^u}$ and the shift $\log(aa')$, proving the homomorphism law. Strong continuity follows by separating the translation and multiplication factors, using strong continuity of $L^2$ translations and dominated convergence for the multipliers. Any bounded commutant operator commutes with $M_{\cos(e^u/n)}$ and $M_{\sin(e^u/n)}$ for each positive integer $n$, because these are the real and imaginary parts of its commuting unitary multipliers at $b=1/n$. These bounded real functions generate the Borel sigma-algebra: $n\sin(e^u/n)\to e^u$, so $u$ is measurable in the generated sigma-algebra, while all the functions are Borel. Thus the exact hypothesis of the multiplication helper is satisfied, and the operator is a multiplication $M_m$ by [[lem-operators-commuting-with-a-point-separating-family-of-multiplications-are-multiplications]]. Commuting with all shifts forces $m(u+h)=m(u)$ a.e. for every $h$. For completeness, convolve $m\in L^\infty$ with a nonnegative unit-mass compactly supported approximate identity: each convolution is continuous and translation invariant, hence constant. Weak-* convergence of these convolutions to $m$ (the $L^1$ approximate-identity property) then shows $\int mf=0$ for every $f\in L^1$ of integral zero, because each constant convolution has that property. Choose one $f_0$ of integral $1$ and put $c=\int mf_0$; subtracting $(\int f)f_0$ from arbitrary $f$ gives $\int mf=c\int f$, hence $m=c$ a.e. Thus the commutant is scalar. A proper invariant closed subspace would have an orthogonal projection commuting with the unitary group (its orthogonal complement is invariant too), giving a nonscalar commutant projection; therefore $\pi$ is irreducible. It acts on infinite-dimensional $L^2(\mathbb R)$ and is inequivalent to every character.

Fix $t$, put $I_R=[-R,-R/2]$ and $\eta_R(u)=(R/2)^{-1/2}e^{itu}\mathbf1_{I_R}(u)$. For $h=\log a$, its unit coefficient is $a^{it}(2/R)\int_{I_R\cap(I_R-h)}e^{ibe^u}\,du$. If $|h|\le L$, $|b|\le B$ and $R>2L$, the intersection has length $R/2-|h|$. Consequently the error from $a^{it}$ is at most $2L/R+B e^{-R/2}$: the first term is the missing overlap mass and the second uses $|e^{ibe^u}-1|\le|b|e^u$ and $u\le-R/2$ on the intersection. This tends to zero uniformly on every compact subset of $G$. Since every coefficient of the one-dimensional $\chi_t$ is a nonnegative multiple of $\chi_t$, these approximations prove $\chi_t\prec\pi$. By [[lem-fell-closure-of-a-single-representation-is-its-weak-containment-closure]], $\chi_t\in\overline{\{\pi\}}$. In particular $1_G\ne\pi$ belongs to that closure, so $\{\pi\}$ is not closed; every singleton of a Hausdorff space is closed, hence $\widehat G$ is not Hausdorff. The source's full affine-group enumeration concerns a different group ($a\in\mathbb R^*$), and is not consumed. AC is inherited from the multiplication, projection, approximate-identity and Fell suppliers and declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

items.title: Fell convergence of the characters of the real line
items.statement: Assume AC. For $G=\mathbb R$, the unitary dual is $\{\chi_t:t\in\mathbb R\}$ with $\chi_t(x)=e^{itx}$, and a net $\chi_{t_i}$ converges to $\chi_t$ in the Fell topology if and only if $t_i\to t$ in $\mathbb R$. For characters, $\chi_s\prec\chi_t$ if and only if $s=t$.
items.strategy: For abelian $G$, every $\pi(g)$ of an irreducible representation is a bounded self-intertwiner, so [[thm-schurs-lemma-for-unitary-representations]] makes it scalar. Every one-dimensional subspace is then invariant, and irreducibility forces dimension one. Thus all irreducibles of $\mathbb R$ are precisely the exponentials from [[lem-continuous-characters-of-the-real-line-are-exponentials]]. A positive-type coefficient of $\chi_t$ is $c\chi_t$, $c\ge0$. Including $0$ in the compact test set forces the approximating scalar sums for a normalized coefficient to converge to $1$. The Fell basis therefore identifies Fell convergence of these characters with compact-uniform convergence. If $t_i\to t$, $|e^{it_ix}-e^{itx}|\le|t_i-t||x|$ gives uniform convergence on bounded compact sets. Conversely let $d_i=t_i-t$ and fix $\delta>0$. On $[-\pi/\delta,\pi/\delta]$, if $|d_i|\ge\delta$, take $x_i=\pi/|d_i|$ to get $|e^{id_ix_i}-1|=2$; uniform convergence rules this out eventually. Hence $d_i\to0$, for nets as well as sequences. Finally, weak containment in a single character approximates $\chi_s$ by $c\chi_t$ with $c\to1$ at $0$, so $\chi_s=\chi_t$ pointwise and $s=t$; the converse is immediate. This also agrees with [[lem-fell-closure-of-a-single-representation-is-its-weak-containment-closure]] because singleton characters are closed. AC is inherited from Schur and the Fell suppliers and declared as [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

items.title: Full and reduced group C star algebras of a finite group
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G$ be a finite group. Then $C^*(G)=C^*_r(G)$ as C*-algebras, and both are $*$-isomorphic to the finite-dimensional semisimple algebra $\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat G}\operatorname{End}(H_\pi)\cong\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat G}M_{d_\pi}(\mathbb C)$, where $d_\pi=\dim H_\pi$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** AC, a finite group $G$, its unitary dual $\widehat G$, the regular representation $\lambda$ and $L^1(G)\subseteq C^*(G)$.

1.1 The evaluation map $\Phi:L^1(G)\to\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat G}\operatorname{End}(H_\pi)$, $f\mapsto(\pi(f))_{\pi\in\widehat G}$, is injective and $\ast$-multiplicative. It is $\ast$-multiplicative by [F3]; for injectivity suppose $\pi(f)=0$ for every $\pi\in\widehat G$. Then every matrix element $\langle\pi(f)e_j,e_i\rangle$ vanishes, and these are $(1/\sqrt{d_\pi})\int_G f(g)u^\pi_{ji}(g)\,d\mu(g)$, the inner products of $f$ with $\overline{u^\pi_{ji}}$ up to nonzero constants. Conjugation sends the complete orthonormal family of [F2] to another complete orthonormal family: it preserves norms and turns each inner product into its conjugate. Hence vanishing of all these inner products forces $f=0$. [F2, F3]

2.1 $\Phi$ is bijective. It is injective by step 1.1, $\dim L^1(G)=|G|$ for the finite group, and the orthonormal basis of [F2] is indexed by the triples $(\pi,i,j)$, so $\sum_{\pi\in\widehat G}d_\pi^2=|G|=\dim L^2(G)$ [F2]; hence the two finite-dimensional spaces have equal dimension and $\Phi$ is a linear isomorphism. Consequently $\Phi$ is a $\ast$-isomorphism of $L^1(G)$ onto the finite-dimensional C\*-algebra $\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat G}\operatorname{End}(H_\pi)$, and it is isometric for the transported norm $\|f\|_\Phi:=\|\Phi(f)\|=\max_{\pi\in\widehat G}\|\pi(f)\|$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The full and reduced norms coincide on $L^1(G)$. By [F4] $\|f\|_{C^*}=\sup_\rho\|\rho(f)\|$ over all unitary representations $\rho$; by [F1] each $\rho$ is a discrete direct sum $\widehat\bigoplus_i\sigma_i$ of irreducibles, so $\|\rho(f)\|=\sup_i\|\sigma_i(f)\|$ and therefore $\sup_\rho\|\rho(f)\|=\max_{\pi\in\widehat G}\|\pi(f)\|=\|f\|_\Phi$. By [F2] $\lambda\cong\widehat\bigoplus_\pi d_\pi\pi$, so also $\|\lambda(f)\|=\max_\pi\|\pi(f)\|=\|f\|_\Phi$; as $C^*_r(G)$ is the completion of $\lambda(L^1(G))$, its norm on $L^1(G)$ is $\|f\|_\Phi$ as well. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 The canonical surjection $C^*(G)\twoheadrightarrow C^*_r(G)$ of [F4] is isometric on the dense image of $L^1(G)$ by step 3.1, hence is injective on a dense subspace and therefore an isometric isomorphism of C\*-algebras; both algebras are the completion of $L^1(G)$ in the common norm $\|\cdot\|_\Phi$. That completion is $L^1(G)$ itself, because step 2.1 exhibits it as isometric to the finite-dimensional, hence complete, algebra $\bigoplus_\pi\operatorname{End}(H_\pi)$. Therefore $C^*(G)=C^*_r(G)\cong\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat G}\operatorname{End}(H_\pi)\cong\bigoplus_{\pi\in\widehat G}M_{d_\pi}(\mathbb C)$ by [F5], a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra with one matrix block per irreducible class. [F4, F5, step 3.1]

5.1 The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the Peter-Weyl decomposition, the representation correspondence and the group C\*-algebra constructions; the dimension count and the norm comparison add no further choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). [given] ∎

items.title: Unitary dual and full group C star algebra of the integers
items.statement: Assume AC. For $G=\mathbb Z$, $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ is the circle group $\mathbb T$ of continuous characters $\chi_z(n)=z^n$, $C^*(\mathbb Z)\cong C(\mathbb T)$, and $C^*_r(\mathbb Z)\cong C(\mathbb T)$ as well; the isomorphism sends $\delta_1$ to the function $z\mapsto z$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** AC, the group $\mathbb Z$, its regular representation $\lambda$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$ and the shift $U=\lambda(1)$.

1.1 By [F1], $\widehat{\mathbb Z}=\{\chi_z:z\in\mathbb T\}$ with $\chi_z(n)=z^n$. By [F2] the Gelfand transform is an isometric $\ast$-isomorphism $C^*(\mathbb Z)\to C_0(\widehat{\mathbb Z})=C(\mathbb T)$, and under the identification $\widehat{\mathbb Z}\cong\mathbb T$ of [F1] the class of $\delta_1$ is sent to the function $\gamma\mapsto\gamma(1)$, that is to $z\mapsto z$; this proves the full-algebra statement. [F1, F2]

1.2 The operator $U$ is unitary and $(U\xi)(k)=\xi(k-1)$, and $\sigma(U)\subseteq\mathbb T$. Unitarity gives $\|U\|=\|U^{-1}\|=1$. If $|\lambda|>1$, then $U-\lambda I=-\lambda(I-\lambda^{-1}U)$ with $\|\lambda^{-1}U\|=|\lambda|^{-1}<1$, so $U-\lambda I$ is invertible by [F4]; if $0<|\lambda|<1$, then $U-\lambda I=U(I-\lambda U^{-1})$ with $\|\lambda U^{-1}\|=|\lambda|<1$, so it is invertible by [F4]; and $\lambda=0$ gives the invertible operator $U$. Hence $\sigma(U)\subseteq\mathbb T$. [F3, F4]

2.1 Conversely $\mathbb T\subseteq\sigma(U)$. For $z\in\mathbb T$ and $N\ge0$ put $\eta_N(k)=z^{-k}\mathbf 1_{[-N,N]}(k)/\sqrt{2N+1}$, a unit vector in $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$; then $(U\eta_N)(k)=z\,z^{-k}\mathbf 1_{[-N,N]}(k-1)/\sqrt{2N+1}$, so $(U-zI)\eta_N$ has support in the two endpoints $\{-N,N+1\}$ and $\|(U-zI)\eta_N\|^2=2/(2N+1)\to0$. If $U-zI$ were invertible with inverse $S$, then $1=\|\eta_N\|\le\|S\|\,\|(U-zI)\eta_N\|\to0$, a contradiction; hence $z\in\sigma(U)$ and $\sigma(U)=\mathbb T$ by step 1.2. [F4, step 1.2]

3.1 The continuous functional calculus of the normal operator $U$ with $\sigma(U)=\mathbb T$ gives an isometric unital $\ast$-isomorphism $C(\mathbb T)\to C^*(I,U)$ sending the coordinate function $z\mapsto z$ to $U$; here $C^*(I,U)$ is the closed span of the powers $U^n$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, because $U^{-1}=U^*$. For $f\in L^1(\mathbb Z)$ the integrated form is $\lambda(f)=\sum_nf(n)U^n$; finitely supported $f$ give finite Laurent polynomials in $U$ and are dense in $L^1(\mathbb Z)=\ell^1(\mathbb Z)$, so by continuity of the integrated form the reduced group C\*-algebra $C^*_r(\mathbb Z)=\overline{\{\lambda(f)\}}$ equals $C^*(I,U)\cong C(\mathbb T)$. Under this isomorphism the image of the group element $\delta_1$ is $\lambda(\delta_1)=\lambda(1)=U$ and hence to the coordinate function $z\mapsto z$. [F3, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the abelian duality corollary, the representation correspondence and the functional calculus; the shift computation and the spectral argument add no further choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). [given] ∎
